Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

14 15 Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to 16 [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of 17 a special protocol. 18 19 If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge 20 conflict, then dstask is for you! 21 22 https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc 23 24 [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) 25 26 ## Features 27 28 - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) 29 - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! 30 - Task listing won't break with long task text 31 - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** 32 - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser 33 - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows 34 - A single statically-linked binary 35 - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. 36 37 ## Non-features 38 39 - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for 40 projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial 41 to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a 42 multi-person project tracked elsewhere. 43 44 ## Requirements 45 46 - Git 47 - A 256-color capable terminal 48 49 ## Installation 50 51 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. 52 - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). 53 - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 54 1. Enable shell completions: 55 - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. 56 - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. 57 - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 58 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 59 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: 60 - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` 61 - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` 62 63 ## PowerShell completion 64 65 Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: 66 67 ```powershell 68 dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 69 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' 70 ``` 71 72 ## Usage 73 74 Run `dstask help` for usage information. 75 76 ### Basic Commands 77 78 - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task 79 - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on 80 - `dstask start` - Start working on a task 81 - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task 82 - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete 83 - `dstask edit` - Edit a task 84 - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task 85 - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note 86 - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks 87 - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks 88 - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks 89 - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) 90 - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote 91 92 ### Task Properties 93 94 - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) 95 - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` 96 - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` 97 - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` 98 - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved 99 100 ### Contexts 101 102 Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: 103 104 ```bash 105 dstask context work 106 dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work 107 dstask # shows only work tasks 108 dstask context -- # clear context 109 ``` 110 111 ### Git Sync 112 113 Sync your tasks across devices using git: 114 115 ```bash 116 # Set up sync on first device 117 cd ~/.dstask 118 git remote add origin 119 git push -u origin master 120 121 # On other devices 122 git clone ~/.dstask 123 124 # To sync 125 dstask sync 126 ``` 127 128 ### Templates 129 130 Create task templates for recurring patterns: 131 132 ```bash 133 dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 134 dstask add from-template 135 ``` 136 137 ## Best Practices 138 139 - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. 140 - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. 141 - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. 142 - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. 143 - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. 144 - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. 145 - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. 146 - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks 147 - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task 148 - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! 149 - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell 164 wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: 165 166 ```bash 167 function dstask () { 168 local has_double_dash subcommand 169 170 if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then 171 has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" 172 subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" 173 if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ 174 [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] 175 then 176 command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ 177 | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ 178 | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ 179 | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" 180 return 181 fi 182 fi 183 184 command dstask "$@" 185 } 186 ``` 187 188 The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` 189 command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All 190 other commands are passed directly to dstask. 191 192 ## Alternatives 193 194 Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. 195 196 - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell 197 - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue 198 - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support 199 - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) 200 - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager 201 - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy 202 203 ## FAQ 204 205 > Does dstask encrypt tasks? 206 207 Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. Note that dstask has not been 211 tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the 212 tools themselves. 213 214 > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? 215 216 Yes. 217 218 1. Set a context: 219 2. Run a modify command without and ID 220 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context 221 222 This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before 223 modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of 224 potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. 225 226 You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. 227 228 > Is there a GUI or web interface? 229 230 Not as part of dstask itself. ### 3g. `dstask undo 1 extra` — extra args silently ignored; reverts HEAD.

### 3h. Dirty working tree

- Dirty files NOT touched by the revert range: undo succeeds, dirty changes survive.
- Revert needs to modify/delete a dirty file: exit 1, no reverts happen, stderr:

  ```
  error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
  	pending/da8445d6-8ab8-40c3-93d3-058931df09ca.yml
  Please commit your changes or stash them before you merge.
  Aborting
  fatal: revert failed
  \x1b[31mFailed to run git cmd.\x1b[0m
  ```

### 3i. undo does not touch `.git/dstask/` (ids.bin/state.bin unchanged) and does not
load tasks (no task-parse errors possible from it). IDs shown inside reverted commit
messages are just the old commit subjects, never recomputed.

## 4. `.git/dstask/` directory

Lives INSIDE `.git`, so it is never committed and never synced. Contains at most two
files, both Go `encoding/gob` blobs:

- `ids.bin` — gob type `IdsMap` = `map[string]int` (UUID → numeric ID).
  Hex dump pattern (1 task): `15 ff 04 01 01 06 49 64 73 4d 61 70 01 ff 80 00 01 0c 01 04 00 00
  <len> ff 80 00 01 24 <36-char UUID> <id*2>` — string type 0x24 = 36 bytes;
  gob zig-zag encodes id n as byte 2n (id 1 → 0x02, 2 → 0x04, 3 → 0x06).
  Map iteration order in the file is not sorted.
- `state.bin` — gob type `State` with one field `Context` of type `Query`.
  The Query struct's gob field list (visible verbatim in the bytes):
  `Cmd string; IDs []int; Tags []string; AntiTags []string; Project string;
  AntiProjects []string; Due Time; DateFilter string; Priority string; Template bool;
  Text string; IgnoreContext bool; Note string`.
  With context `+work project:proj` set, the payload ends with `... 01 07 63 6f 6e 74 65 78 74
  02 01 04 77 6f 72 6b 02 04 70 72 6f 6a 00 00` i.e. Cmd="context", Tags=["work"],
  Project="proj". With `context none`, the Context payload is empty (file shrinks to
  the type-definition preamble only).

When written:
- `ids.bin` is (re)written by task-mutating commands (add/start/stop/done/modify/
  remove/log/template/note/edit...). Pure reads (next/show-*/context query) and the
  git commands (`git`, `sync`, `undo`) do NOT write it — observed unchanged after
  `sync` pulled in a new remote task, and after `show-open`.
- `state.bin` is written by `context <filter>` (and `context none`). `context` makes
  NO git commit and prints nothing on set; `context` with no args prints the current
  context to stdout, e.g. `+work project:proj\n` (empty line when none), exit 0.

ID assignment semantics (deduced): on load, each on-disk task keeps its saved id from
ids.bin if its UUID is present; tasks not in the map get the lowest positive integer
not used by any other loaded task. Stale map entries for vanished tasks are dropped at
the next save. Verified: after externally deleting task A (id 1) and committing, a new
`add` printed `Added 1: C` and reused id 1. After a `sync` merge, the pulled-in remote
task (unknown UUID) got id 1 while a local task kept its saved id 2.

Corrupt task files: a `.yml` that fails to parse is silently skipped by all
task-loading commands; a Go-log-formatted line goes to stderr:
`2026/08/07 20:15:17 error loading task: failed to unmarshal 973ff73d-b9bf-4608-b37e-2baf8e292c36.yml`
(`log` package default: `YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS `). JSON list output is then just `[]`
(no trailing newline). Consequence: an unparseable file frees its ID for reuse by the
next `add`.

## 5. Commit behaviour of mutation commands

- Every mutation = ONE git commit per affected task (batch `dstask 1 2 done` makes two
  separate commits, `Resolved 1: b1` then `Resolved 2: b2`).
- The commit stages **ALL** worktree changes, not just the task file — equivalent to
  `git add -A` + `git commit -m <msg>`. Verified twice: an unrelated dirty tracked
  file AND unrelated untracked files (`random-junk.txt`, `pending/not-a-task.txt`)
  were swept into an `Added` commit.
- Commit output (`[master abc1234] msg` + stat lines) is wrapped in grey:
  `\x1b[38;5;245m` ... `\x1b[0m`, printed to **stdout**, with NO trailing newline
  after the reset code (exact tail: `...yml\n\x1b[0m`). The human line before it is
  preceded by a blank line. Full byte pattern for `add`:

  ```
  \nAdded 2: second\n\x1b[38;5;245m[master 3afa370] Added 2: second\n 1 file changed, 11 insertions(+)\n create mode 100644 pending/09ea1e1b-....yml\n\x1b[0m
  ```

- Nothing-to-commit case (e.g. `edit` saved without changes): prints
  `\nEdited 1: edited summary\n\x1b[38;5;245mNo changes detected\n\x1b[0m`, exit 0, no commit.

### Exact commit message formats (all verified in `git log`)

| command | stdout human line | commit message |
|---|---|---|
| `add Fix things` | `Added 1: Fix things` | `Added 1: Fix things` |
| `start Fix things` (add+start) | `Added and started 3: Fix things` | `Added and started 3: Fix things` |
| `2 start` | `Started 2: task two` | `Started 2: task two` |
| `2 stop [note]` | `Stopped 2: task two` | `Stopped 2: task two` |
| `1 done [note]` | `Resolved 1: task one` | `Resolved 1: task one` |
| `1 modify +tag` | `Modified 1: task one` | `Modified 1: task one` |
| `3 remove` | `3: task three...` then `Removed: 3: task three...` | `Removed: 3: task three started immediately` (note the colon after `Removed`) |
| `log Some task` | `Logged Some task` | `Logged logged task` (no ID, format `Logged <summary>`) |
| `template Foo` | `Created Template 1: Foo` | `Created Template 1: Foo` |
| `1 edit` (editor) | `Edited 1: edited summary` | `Edited 1: edited summary` (new summary) |
| `1 note ...` | `Edit note 1: n task` | `Edit note 1: n task` |
| `context <f>` | (no output) | NO COMMIT |
| sync merge | (git output) | `Merge branch 'master' of /tmp/remote` (git default) |
| `undo` | (git output) | `Revert "<original subject>"` |

Notes on specific commands:
- `remove` stdout is: `<id>: <summary>\n` `\nRemoved: <id>: <summary>\n` then grey commit block.
- `note`/`edit` open `$EDITOR` on a temp file `/tmp/dstask.<pid>.<id>-<slug>.md`
  (note) / `...yml` (edit). **Without a TTY (and without DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1) `note`
  silently does NOTHING: no editor, no append, no commit, exit 0.** With
  `DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1` (or a real TTY) it works: inline text (`dstask 1 note some text`)
  is appended and committed with message `Edit note <id>: <summary>`.
- `edit` with an editor that corrupts the YAML: stdout
  `Failed to unmarshal yaml: line 14: could not find expected ':'` then prompt
  `Try again? [y/n] ` — with stdin at EOF it **panics**: `panic: EOF` + goroutine
  stack, exit code **2**.
- `done`/`stop` with trailing text append the text to the task's `notes:` field in the
  same commit (notes become a YAML block: `notes: |2-\n\n  closing note`).
- `context` never commits (state lives in `.git/dstask/state.bin` only).

## 6. Repository auto-initialisation & errors

- If `DSTASK_GIT_REPO` does not exist, ANY command auto-creates it: `mkdir -p` +
  `git init` (output streamed through: `Initialized empty Git repository in .../.git/`
  on stdout, git's `hint:` lines on stderr), then prints to stdout:

  ```
  \nAdd a remote repository with:\n\n\tdstask git remote add origin <repo>\n\n
  ```

  then the command's normal output (e.g. `[]` for `next`, no trailing newline). Exit 0.
  No status dirs, no `.git/dstask/` at this point — the 8 status directories
  (`pending`, `active`, `paused`, `resolved`, `template`, `deferred`, `delegated`,
  `recurring`, mode 0700) are created lazily on first task write.
- If the directory exists but is NOT a git repo (no `.git`): exit **1**, stderr only:
  `\x1b[31mFailed to create directory in git repository\x1b[0m` (no trailing newline).
  Same for every command tried (`git status`, `add`).

## 7. Task YAML file format (for reference)

`<status>/<uuid>.yml`, UUID v4 lowercase. Field order fixed:

```yaml
summary: first task
notes: ""
tags: []
project: ""
priority: P2
delegatedto: ""
subtasks: []
dependencies: []
created: 2026-08-07T20:03:43.415930394Z
resolved: 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z
due: 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z
```

Timestamps: RFC3339 with nanoseconds, UTC `Z` (`2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999Z07:00`
Go format — variable fractional digits). Zero time rendered as `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z`.
Status is encoded by the directory; moving pending→active→paused→resolved shows as
git renames (`rename {pending => active}/<uuid>.yml`). `log` writes directly into
`resolved/` with `resolved` set to the same instant as `created`.

## 8. Rule summary for reimplementation

1. `git` cmd: spawn `git <args>` in repo, inherit stdio, exit 0 on success; on failure
   stderr += red `Failed to run git cmd.`, exit 1.
2. `sync`: `git pull --ff --no-rebase --no-edit --commit` then `git push`; stop at
   first failure (same red-error/exit-1 contract). No dstask-specific output at all.
3. `undo [n]`: `git revert --no-edit HEAD~<n>..` (n default 1; non-numeric → usage to
   stderr, exit 0). Never rewrites history; can never touch the root commit.
4. Mutation commands commit with `git add -A`-style staging of EVERYTHING and print
   `<blank>\n<Human line>\n` + grey-wrapped commit output (no trailing newline).
5. `.git/dstask/ids.bin` (gob map UUID→id) and `.git/dstask/state.bin` (gob State with
   Context Query) are local-only, never committed, written only by mutations/context.
6. All git-failure paths converge on: stream git output, red `Failed to run git cmd.`
   to stderr, exit 1.
